source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan & Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure, Psychological Review
finding: Review argues most amnesia-type deficits (drugs or new events after training or after reactivation) can be reversed by suitable retrieval cues. The post-training manipulation is said to create new learning that interferes with the original memory, so recall becomes highly cue-dependent.
numbers: No effect sizes or study counts in the record page. DOI 10.1037/rev0000538, PMID 39977697. Scopus lists 6 citations.
quote: memory retrieval is a critical component of memory performance
limits: Only the abstract and record page were read, not the full text. The authors (Miller, Ryan) are long-time proponents, so this is advocacy, not a neutral count. Narrative review, no stated search protocol.
agent_relevance: Target claim of this subfield. Treat 'memory not found' as a possible cue failure first, and try other cues before concluding the item is absent.

source: Ryan, Roy, Pignatelli, Arons & Tonegawa (2015) Engram cells retain memory under retrograde amnesia, Science
finding: Mice given anisomycin after contextual fear training froze less to natural cues, but optogenetic activation of the tagged dentate gyrus engram cells still produced freezing. The memory was stored but not reachable by natural cues.
numbers: Natural recall: anisomycin group froze less than saline (Test 1 p<0.005; Test 2 p<0.05). Light-induced freezing: saline p<0.01, anisomycin p<0.05, no group difference. DG place avoidance n=10 ANI, 12 SAL. CA1 n=9/10, lateral amygdala n=9/9. Freezing percentages are in figures only, not in the text read.
limits: One drug, one task, male mice, small groups (3 to 12). Optogenetic recall is artificial and may differ from natural recall. Anisomycin dose not stated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct demonstration that failed natural retrieval does not mean absent trace. For an LLM agent: a missing answer under one prompt is weak evidence the knowledge is gone.

source: Roy et al. (2017) Silent memory engrams as the basis for retrograde amnesia, PNAS
finding: Anisomycin-treated mice still show freezing by optogenetic recall of DG engram cells at 2, 5 and 8 days, while natural recall is lost. The engram keeps cell-to-cell connectivity but loses the learning-induced spine increase. Restoring spine density (PAK1 over-expression in CA1) restored natural recall.
numbers: Optogenetic recall n: 2 d saline 10 / ani 12; 5 d 9/10; 8 d 9/8. Anisomycin 150 mg/kg. Laser 25% power (1.5-2.5 mW): no significant freezing in ANI (n=8); 50% (4-6 mW) and 75% (7-9 mW) significant in both. DG spines: saline 7,045 (7 mice), ani 5,789 (6 mice). PAK1 rescue n=15 per group.
limits: Boundary: the silent state is weak; a strong enough stimulus is needed (25% power fails). Male mice only, one drug, tested only to 8 days, connectivity measured against estimated chance overlap.
agent_relevance: A memory can be present but 'silent' (weak path), so cue strength matters, not only cue presence. Suggests escalating cue strength rather than retrying one weak cue.

source: Gisquet-Verrier, Lynch, Cutolo, Toledano, Ulmen, Jasnow & Riccio (2015) Integration of new information with active memory accounts for retrograde amnesia, J Neurosci
finding: Rival to consolidation theory. Amnesia after cycloheximide or LiCl in rat inhibitory avoidance is reversed by a reminder or by re-giving the drug before test. This fits a state-dependent retrieval failure, not a lost trace. LiCl causes amnesia without inhibiting protein synthesis.
numbers: Exp 1a Cyclo vs Sal F(1,15)=28.39 p<0.001, re-dosing and reminder reversed it. Exp 1b F(1,16)=43.67; re-dosing partial F(1,18)=5.41 p=0.03. Exp 2a F(1,17)=8.78 p<0.01, none at 6 h delay. Exp 4 intrahippocampal F(1,11)=22.51, reversed by pre-test infusion F(1,12)=16.34. Cyclo cut protein synthesis 72% at 30 min; LiCl raised it 3-5%. Groups 5 to 11.
limits: Authors admit integration is inferred, not shown. Small groups, two labs with different protocols, LiCl malaise confound, dose dependence, some reported stats inconsistent (Exp 1a F=6.20 with p=0.23). Rats, one task. Read via a summarising fetch tool, so numbers are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Amnesic drug as 'internal state' maps to context or mode: a model that learned in one frame may need that frame restored at test. Reinstating the original frame can be a retrieval aid.

source: Sarma et al. (2026) Restoring access to long-term social recognition memories disrupted by sleep deprivation, Science Advances
finding: Six hours of sleep deprivation after socialization left mice unable to recognise partner mice next day. Optogenetic reactivation of tagged DG engram cells restored recognition. The PDE4 inhibitor roflumilast given before the test restored it only temporarily.
numbers: n = 9 to 12 per group. Sleep-deprived mice kept preferring the stimulus mouse (failed recognition); ChR2+ mice showed no preference (recognised), ChR2- controls kept the preference. Sleep deprivation did not change engram formation or overlap; only experience-specific reactivation fell.
limits: Male mice, one social paradigm. Authors say the key claim is sufficiency, not selectivity. Statistics table (S1) not read. Roflumilast rescue is transient. No human test.
agent_relevance: Another case where forgetting looks like lost access with intact encoding. A retrieval-time intervention beats re-training.

source: Sarma et al. (2026), alternative-explanation controls
finding: Controls rule out simple non-memory explanations: sleep deprivation came after socialization, not before testing, and total social exploration at test was not reduced. Authors cite earlier work against a stress or glucocorticoid explanation.
numbers: Total exploration at test not reduced in sleep-deprived mice. Impairment showed as more exploration of the stimulus mouse, not less.
limits: Stress argument rests on earlier studies; stress was not measured here.
agent_relevance: Before concluding 'retrieval failure', rule out a non-memory cause. This control logic is a model for agent self-checks and evaluation.

source: Pigeon, Lonergan, Rotondo et al. (2022) Impairing memory reconsolidation with propranolol in healthy and clinical samples: a meta-analysis, J Psychiatry Neurosci
finding: Meta-analysis of the human reconsolidation-blockade claim, the main rival to retrieval failure for post-reactivation amnesia. Propranolol at reactivation reduced recall and fear in healthy adults and symptoms in clinical samples.
numbers: Healthy adults Hedges g = -0.51 (p=0.002); clinical (PTSD, addiction, phobia) g = -0.42 (p=0.010). 14 healthy and 12 clinical studies pooled; 618 propranolol vs 527 placebo participants across all included studies. 8 of 11 differential fear-conditioning studies in healthy people found effects.
limits: Methodological heterogeneity; mixed outcomes (physiology versus symptoms). Challenged by Steenen et al. A drug effect alone cannot separate erased trace from cue-dependent retrieval failure.
agent_relevance: A manipulation after reactivation changes later expression. Whether that is erasure or retrieval failure is the dispute the 2025 review takes up.

source: Steenen, van Westrhenen, de Lange & de Jongh (2022) Updated and rectified meta-analysis shows no effect of propranolol versus placebo on traumatic memory reconsolidation disruption, J Psychiatry Neurosci
finding: Re-analysis of Pigeon et al. Three unpublished trials were missed, two trials used physiology not symptoms, and five addiction studies are mechanistically different. Restricted to low-risk-of-bias RCTs in psychotrauma, propranolol was not significantly better than placebo; adding newer trials widened the interval.
numbers: Pooled g not in text read (forest plots only). Counts: 14 healthy studies and 12 RCTs in the original, 3 missed unpublished trials, 5 substance studies.
limits: Short letter, numbers in figures not read. The original authors replied in a separate letter. Clinical trials differ from lab studies.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication style evidence: a headline reversible-memory intervention shrinks under strict inclusion. Treat large claimed effects as fragile until independent.

source: Pigeon et al. (2022) versus Steenen et al. (2022) contrast
finding: Two analyses of nearly the same studies disagree: clinical g=-0.42 (significant) versus no significant benefit once low-risk-of-bias RCTs and missed unpublished trials are used. Inclusion rules drive the answer.
numbers: Pigeon: clinical g=-0.42 p=0.010; healthy g=-0.51 p=0.002. Steenen: restricted pooled analysis not significant.
limits: Exact Steenen estimate not read. Not a final verdict.
agent_relevance: Weigh each reported rescue effect by risk of bias, not by headline.

source: Noradrenergic blockade of memory reconsolidation: a failure to reduce conditioned fear responding (2014), Front Behav Neurosci (authors not verified)
finding: Failed replication in healthy humans. Spider pictures paired with shock; 40 mg propranolol before reactivation did not reduce fear-potentiated startle at reinstatement, unlike the group's earlier findings.
numbers: N = 44 undergraduates (16 men, 28 women, mean age 20.66). Propranolol lowered blood pressure as expected: systolic t(43)=10.54 d=1.59, diastolic t(43)=4.89 d=1.27. Trait anxiety, spider fear and BP did not predict fear retention or reinstatement.
limits: Design had a propranolol condition compared with earlier data, no concurrent placebo arm seen in the text read. First-author name not checked.
agent_relevance: Boundary: the blockable-memory effect is not reliable even with the drug that first showed it. Do not build a mechanism on one effect.

source: Genuine memory deficits assessed by the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test in behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia: meta-analysis (2024)
finding: Boundary for 'amnesia is a cue problem'. The FCSRT gives cues at encoding and at recall to separate storage failure from retrieval failure. bvFTD patients stay clearly impaired even with cueing, so the deficit is not only retrieval.
numbers: 16 studies. Total delayed recall (cued) bvFTD vs controls: effect -1.25 (95% CI -1.51 to -0.98), 209 patients, 235 controls, 8 studies. Free immediate recall -1.98 (CI -2.30 to -1.65), 271 patients, 520 controls, 7 studies. Egger tests not significant.
limits: Heterogeneous studies; hippocampal atrophy in bvFTD resembles Alzheimer's disease, so low cued recall may reflect real storage damage. Human clinical, not engram work.
agent_relevance: Cues help only when the item was encoded. An agent should separate 'never stored' (no cue helps) from 'stored but unreachable' by testing several cue types.

source: Kotha, Springer & Raghunathan (2024) Understanding catastrophic forgetting in language models via implicit inference, ICLR
finding: Fine-tuning seems to destroy abilities, but the ability is often still there and the model infers the wrong task. Conjugate prompting (making the prompt look unlike the fine-tuning data, for example by translating it) brings back the suppressed capability.
numbers: In-context learning drops after fine-tuning: Alpaca 56.75% fewer inputs than LLaMa-7b, Vicuna-7b 40.00% fewer, OPT-IML-1.3b 21.00% fewer than OPT-1.3b. After English code fine-tuning, Code LLaMa is 8.36% worse on English XNLI but within 2% in French, Spanish and German.
quote: fine-tuning skews task inference towards the fine-tuning distribution
limits: Refusal-task numbers (Table 3) not extracted. Synthetic regression is a toy. Recovery is partial. The authors note code training may also help non-English accuracy.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of retrieval failure: a reframed cue recovers a lost skill. Try cue variants before declaring a capability absent.

source: Deeb & Roger (2025) Do unlearning methods remove information from language model weights?
finding: Test of removed versus hidden. Fine-tuning an unlearned Llama 3 8B on some facts T recovers other, disjoint facts V. Recovery rate exceeds 88% of pre-unlearning accuracy for knowledge learned in pretraining (RMU, gradient difference, RIA).
numbers: Years, MMLU, WMDP-Deduped: recovery rate at least 88%. Each split 157 items; 4 splits (628) for retraining, 1 for test; 2 runs. Random Birthdays (knowledge added by fine-tuning): high recovery for RMU, but GD and RIA under 35%.
limits: One main model (Llama 3 8B), one fine-tuned dataset. Retraining could teach, not only uncover; disjoint facts reduce this. Unlearning strength capped at 5% retain-accuracy drop.
agent_relevance: Pretrained knowledge behaves as hidden-not-removed under suppression, which fits the retrieval-failure reading. Boundary: knowledge added only by fine-tuning was largely truly removed.

source: Deeb & Roger (2025), format and robustness checks
finding: Recovery depends on matching format and granularity between unlearning data, retraining data and test. GD works best when all three use the multiple-choice format. Even with strong damage to other skills, forgotten facts stay recoverable.
numbers: Even when retain accuracy falls to 25%, forget accuracy after retraining stays high on Years. Recovery also seen without a retain loss (Appendix G).
limits: Appendix tables and the granularity stress test were not fully extracted.
agent_relevance: Cue format must match stored format. The same fact asked in another format may not reach the trace.

source: Hu, Fu, Wu & Smith (2025) Unlearning or obfuscating? Jogging the memory of unlearned LLMs via benign relearning, ICLR
finding: Small, loosely related data restores unlearned content. Relearning on public medical articles brings back bioweapon knowledge; wiki text about Harry Potter brings back verbatim memorised text. Authors conclude approximate unlearning suppresses output, not knowledge.
numbers: Keyword attack success above 70% when unlearning is shallow, falling as unlearning goes deeper. On TOFU, more than 40 relearning steps lowered success. Relearn-data relevance test: English text ending in 'Anthony' 100%, English female names 20%, Japanese text 9%, gibberish 9%, none 0%.
limits: Deep unlearning resisted. More relearning steps not always better. Small-number table values read from jumbled PDF layout.
agent_relevance: A related partial cue acts like a reminder; the cue need not match the target. Over-cueing is unreliable.

source: Hu et al. (2025), shallow versus deep and repetition
finding: Return of suppressed content grows with how often the cue is repeated and falls with unlearning depth, on a toy name-pair task.
numbers: Table with shallow (7 steps), medium (12), deep (17) checkpoints: 7 pairs 8%, 48%, 100%; 5 pairs 2%, 17%, 97%; 3 pairs 1%, 1%, 23%; 1 pair 0%, 0%, 0%.
limits: Mapping of columns to checkpoints inferred from jumbled text. Small model, synthetic task.
agent_relevance: Dose-response in cue material: one cue may fail where several succeed.

source: Lucki, Wei, Huang, Henderson, Tramer & Rando (2025) An adversarial perspective on machine unlearning for AI safety, TMLR
finding: Hazardous knowledge removed by RMU, NPO and DPO is recoverable without original data: fine-tuning on 10 unrelated examples, removing activation directions, or universal adversarial prefixes.
numbers: WMDP accuracy after fine-tuning on 10 retain-set samples: NPO 52.7%, DPO 57.0%, RMU 61.6%, MMLU drop under 2 points. RMU orthogonalization 64.7% vs baseline 64.4%. Universal prefixes: RMU 29.9% to 53.9%, NPO 29.5% to 46.0%, DPO 27.9% to 49.0%.
limits: Several attacks need white-box access and the pre-unlearning model for reference.
agent_relevance: A few-token cue can flip a suppressed model back to answering. Retrieval gating can sit in a narrow direction.

source: Lucki et al. (2025), method and format differences
finding: Recovery varies by method and prompt format. NPO and DPO resisted direction ablation more than RMU. RMU ablation worked with the chat template (53.7%) but not without it (34.1%).
numbers: Ablation NPO 45%, DPO 51%, RMU 64.7%. Prefix gap up to 20 points (31.2% without vs 51.4% with chat template).
limits: Context format limits any single recovery recipe.
agent_relevance: Recovery is cue-format sensitive in models, as encoding specificity predicts in people.

source: Lynch, Guo, Ewart, Casper & Hadfield-Menell (2024) Eight methods to evaluate robust unlearning in LLMs
finding: The 'Who's Harry Potter' model looks forgetful but knowledge resurfaces under small fine-tuning on a share of the book corpus.
numbers: Familiarity 77% lower than Llama-2 baseline. Fine-tuning on 800 sentences (about 1% of corpus) and 8,000 sentences (about 10%); the 8,000-sentence run brings the model close to the Llama-2 baseline.
limits: One unlearned model. The 1% run did not reach parity.
agent_relevance: Dose-response with amount of re-exposure.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive interference reveals working memory limits in LLMs beyond context length
finding: The interference side of cue-dependent forgetting. As related key-value updates stream in, retrieval of the latest value falls log-linearly toward zero, even with the answer placed just before the query. Errors are old overwritten values.
numbers: 35 model variants (GPT-4.1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini, Qwen3, Llama 3.1 and 4 and more). Accuracy declines log-linearly with interference load. Prompts telling the model to ignore or forget earlier input gave limited gains.
limits: Synthetic key-value task. Exact slopes and mitigation percentages not extracted.
agent_relevance: Cue overload: one cue pointing at many items defeats retrieval, and 'ignore the old items' instructions do not fix it. Change the cue structure (unique cues, remove stale entries).

source: Patil, Hase & Bansal (2023) Can sensitive information be deleted from LLMs? Objectives for defending against extraction attacks
finding: Model-editing deletion from GPT-J still leaves the answer in hidden states. White-box attacks extract it far more often than output tests suggest.
numbers: White-box attack extracts the deleted answer 38% of the time with budget B=20; black-box paraphrase attack 29%. A new defence cuts white-box success from 38% to 2.4%. GPT-J baseline accuracy 34% (CounterFact) and 25% (zsRE).
limits: One model (GPT-J), narrow fact edits. Defence weaker against unseen attack types.
agent_relevance: Early LLM evidence that a model can fail to say what it still represents. Output failure is not proof of absence.

source: Gisquet-Verrier et al. (2015), time gradient and controls
finding: The usual time gradient of amnesia (drug acts only right after training or reactivation) is argued to track how active the memory is when the new state is encoded, not consolidation speed. A drug-novelty control did not remove the effect.
numbers: Cyclo ICV: impairment F(1,14)=10.39 p<0.01, reversed by re-infusion F(1,11)=5.86 p<0.05; no effect at 6 h delay. LiCl after reactivation: immediate impairment F(1,15)=8.25 p<0.01; none at 120 min delay though taste aversion still formed. Drug pre-exposure one week before training: deficit F(1,15)=4.65 p<0.05.
limits: Interpretation disputed; drug malaise remains a confound.
agent_relevance: Timing matters. New text placed right after key facts may interfere more than text added later.

source: Ryan et al. (2015), cell-population and reconsolidation boundaries
finding: Populations differ. CA1 engram stimulation needed a 4 Hz protocol; the standard 20 Hz did not work. After reactivation plus anisomycin (reconsolidation), optogenetic recall also stayed intact at day 4.
numbers: CA1 light-induced freezing: SAL p<0.01, ANI p<0.001 (n=10, 9). Reconsolidation DG: SAL p<0.001, ANI p<0.003 (n=11 per group). Chance overlap CA3 0.76, BLA 0.42.
limits: P values only in the text read; figures not available.
agent_relevance: Cue parameters must match the store; a cue that works in one place fails in another.

source: Miller & Springer (1974) Implications of recovery from experimental amnesia, Psychological Review (snippet record only)
finding: Listed as concluding that retrieval failure is the more plausible reading of reversal of experimental amnesia. The idea is about 50 years old.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Search snippet only, page not opened.
agent_relevance: The claim has been argued for decades and never settled; do not assume consensus.

source: Psychological Review 2025 article, full text (not obtained)
finding: Full text not obtainable (paywalled, no open copy found). The review's own tally of reversal successes versus failures is unknown here.
numbers: Unknown.
limits: Key gap: a count of failures to reverse amnesia is the missing number.
agent_relevance: Cite the review only for its qualitative claim, not for percentages.
